newsitem.title: BOSNIA: World Bank, EU postone Bosnia aid conference.
newsitem.headline: World Bank, EU postone Bosnia aid conference.

text.p: An international fund-raising conference for Bosnia set for next week has been postponed because the peacetime central government failed to adopt economic reforms in time, the World Bank said on Friday.

The conference was delayed until at least mid-July because the inter-ethnic government had failed to make "sufficient progress" in adopting laws proposed by the international community as a precondition for more aid, a statement issued by the World Bank and European Union said.
The announcement was made shortly before the country's parliament finally adopted the package of economic reforms on Friday afternoon, Bosnian state news agency reported.
The vote came too late for the World Bank and the European Commission, which as sponsors of the event needed to confirm invitations on Friday morning, officials said.

"As of this date, the donors' conference has not been rescheduled but, should the recent rapid progress continue, it is expected that it could take place in Brussels before mid-July," EU envoy Donato Chiarini said in the statement.
The conference, which was expected to raise $1.4 billion in reconstruction aid in 1997, has been repeatedly postponed because the central government has failed to approve the reform package.
The reforms include laws on a central bank, budget, foreign debt service, customs and tariff laws which are supposed to steer the country towards a market-oriented economy.

Friday's vote cleared the way for an important agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which is another pre-condition for the aid conference. Western officials said Bosnia's negotiations with the IMF are due to begin immediately to secure the $100 million deal.
The World Bank said the IMF programme was a crucial prerequisite for successful debt negotiations with Paris and London clubs and commercial creditors.

Leaders of Bosnia's Serb republic withrew their support earlier this month for the economic laws which had been agreed after months of negotiations, objecting to a customs law that harmonised rates between Serb and Moslem-Croat terrorities.

Nationalist Serb leaders had opposed the customs and tariffs law because they said it violated a cooperation agreement with neighbouring Yugoslavia. International envoys dismissed the cooperation pact between the Serb entity and Yugoslavia, saying it carried no legal validity.

Details of the customs law passed on Friday had yet to be released but diplomats said the law contained amendments to accommodate Serb objections. The state news agency reported that a commission would work out rates for specific products.
A 1995 peace agreement split Bosnia into autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories governed by a central presidency, cabinet and parliament.
The joint bodies have been plagued by stalemate but the adoption of the reforms marked the first major legislation adopted by the parliament since post-war elections were held last September.
Serb leaders said they expected to obtain more financial aid this year after receiving only about two percent of more than a billion dollars committed to the country in 1996.
Donor countries have linked reconstruction aid to compliance with the Dayton peace agreement and as a result the Serb entity missed out on much of the financial assistance.
